--- title: "4. How Hydrophones Work" --- # General A hydrophone is a device that passively detects acoustic signal underwater. The word *hydrophone* comes from the Greek *hydro* (water), and *phone* (voice). Acoustic data are recorded in the form of a time-amplitude signal, at a specified sampling rate. Several types of hydrophones exist depending on the applications, with different frequency range. Some of the most common applications of **passive acoustics** are: ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} ## Passive acoustics Action of listening to sound without emitting a signal, whereas in active acoustics the emitted signal is then analysed. ::: - marine mammal monitoring - ambient noise characterization - earthquakes detection # From pressure to voltage Hydrophones contain a key element, a **piezoelectric** material, which "feels" the pressure changes of a passing sound wave, and convert them into electric signals. In such, hydrophones are essentially **transducers**, as they simply convert potential energy into electrical energy. ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} ## Piezoelectric Material that generates an electric charge in response to applied mechanical stress. As a wave passes, it compresses the ceramic, which creates a proportional electrical voltage. ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} ## Transducer A device that converts energy from one form (acoustic pressure) to another (electrical voltage). ::: The relationship between the pressure (p) and the voltage (V) is determined by the sensitivity of the hydrophone, usually expressed in dB re 1V/μPa. ![Conversion of sound signal to electric signal.](../images/hydrophone-signal-schematic.png){lightbox=true} The piezoelectric material is often made of ceramics, more specifically Lead-Zirconate-Titanate (PZT) compounds, which are relatively low cost, and have an excellent piezoelectric coefficient. It also has high sensitivity and can operate at wide range of temperatures. The transducer is often shaped as a cylinder or a sphere, which is ideal for listening to signal from all direction. # Sensitivity The sensitivity of the hydrophone refers to how efficient the hydrophone converts underwater sound pressure into an electrical signal. Quantitatively, it is the ratio of sound pressure signal and the output voltage signal: $$ M_\nu = \frac{V_h}{P_h} \ \ ; \ \ \text{units:} \left[ \frac{V}{\mu Pa} \right] $$ What affects hydrophone sensitivity: - **Hydrophone type**: size, design and choice of material (e.g. piezoelectric compound); - **Frequency**: piezoelectric hydrophones have a resonance frequency which depends on the piezoelectric material. Sensitivity is usually good below the resonance frequency and drops rapidly above. - **Environmental conditions**: water temperature, salinity and pressure can substantially impact hydrophone sensitivity. It is important to calibrate the instrument relative to those conditions. Knowing the sensitivity is essential to choose the right hydrophone for the right application. Hydrophones can be separated into three categories with overlapping ranges: - Low-Frequency (Infrasonic): 1 Hz - 1 kHz - Audio-Frequency: 10 Hz - 10 kHz - High-Frequency (Ultrasonic): 10 Hz - 200 kHz ![Sensitivity curve of a high-frequency piezoelectric hydrophone.](../images/sensitivity-curve.png){lightbox=true} # Signal processing methods Several methods are used to convert the recorded electric signal in data we can analyse. One method is **Fourier Analysis**, where the total signal is decomposed into a set individual frequencies with associated phase and amplitudes. ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} ## Fourier analysis Signal decomposition method where a complex signal is expressed as superimposition of simple sine and cosine waves of different frequencies. ::: ![Fourier analysis for signal decomposition. Credit: Medium.](../images/fourier-transform.png){lightbox=true} This way, a time-domain signal is converted into a frequency-domain signal which makes it easier to capture at which frequency most of the energy is. For long periods of sound recording, the signal can be divided into shorter segments of equal lengths, specified by a *time-window*. The result shows how the spectra changes with time, the **spectrogram**. ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} ## Spectrogram A visual, three-dimensional representation of a signal's frequency spectrum as it changes over time. ::: ![Example of a spectrogram: time on the x-axis, frequency in Hz on the y-axis, and colour for sound level.](../images/spectrogram.png){lightbox=true} The x-axis is time, the y-axis represents the frequencies in Hz (per second), while the colours represent the level, expressed in logarithm of the signal power in dB. Note on choosing the window: it’s impossible to have a good resolution in time and frequency at the same time (Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle). - Short window = good time resolution, poor frequency resolution - Long window = good frequency resolution, poor time resolution Hydrophones can be put into three categories, infrasonic, ultrasonic, and ?? ## Signal to noise ratio Signal to Noise ratio is an important element to consider for hydrophones. A bigger element increases sensitivity, but also can lower SNR. A rule of thumb is to ensure the measured amplitude is at least 5 times larger than the noise equavalent pressure (NEP) of the hydrophone to maximize the signal to noise ratio (SNR). $$ NEP [Pa] = \frac{\text{Pre-amp Noise} ~[\mu V]}{\text{Sensitivity} ~[nV~Pa^{-1}] \times \text{Pre-amp Gain}} \times 1000 $$ ![Signal-to-noise ratio measures the desired signal against background noise. Credit: Hollyland.](../images/snr.png){lightbox=true} # Other hydrophone types Several transducer designs can record underwater sound. **Ocean Networks Canada uses piezoelectric hydrophones** (Ocean Sonics icListen and GeoSpectrum elements supplied by JASCO). The rest of this handbook refers to piezoelectric hydrophones unless noted otherwise. ::: {.hydrophone-types-table tbl-colwidths="[18,32,50]"} | Type | Operating principle | Notes | |------|---------------------|-------| | **Piezoelectric** | A ceramic element (typically PZT) produces a voltage proportional to acoustic pressure. | Used throughout the ONC network. Sensitive over a wide band; omnidirectional when the element is a cylinder or sphere. | | **Fiber-optic** | Acoustic pressure modulates light travelling in an optical fibre (interferometry). | Immune to electromagnetic interference; used in some long-range or high-EMI applications. Not used at ONC. | | **Accelerometer / inertial** | Measures particle acceleration or velocity rather than pressure. | Useful as a vector sensor for directionality. Not used as ONC's primary hydrophones. | ::: # Passive acoustics applications Passive acoustic monitoring is often associated with underwater soundscapes, but the same instruments support a wider set of ocean applications, from seismology and tsunami detection to marine mammal monitoring and vessel tracking. The table below groups those applications by frequency band. | Category | Applications | Frequency Range |--------|--------|--------| | **Seismic & Geophysics** | Earthquakes, Tsunami detection, Oil & Gas exploration, Seabed mapping, Subsea leakage. | **Sub Hz - 100 Hz** | | **Biological** | Marine mammal vocalization, Ecosystem studies | **10 Hz - ~200 kHz** | | **Natural Ambient** | Ambient noise monitoring. | **10 Hz - 1000 Hz** | | **Naval & Surveillance** | Submarine/Vessel detection, harbour surveillance. | **3 kHz – 300 kHz** | | **Communication** | Submarine communication, navigation. | **3 Hz – 300 kHz** | ::: {#cell-map-output .cell lightbox='true' execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Comparison of frequency ranges across multidisciplinary hydrophone applications.](4-how-hydrophones-work_files/figure-html/map-output-output-1.png){#map-output width=690 height=389} ::: ::: # Resources - Suedel et al., 2019.
